Recommendations

Every page shows a row of things the visitor might like. A ranking model builds each row, but the model is slow and costly. The row must appear instantly, even when the model is having a bad day. Practise this medium system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

Every page shows a row of things the visitor might like. A ranking model builds each row, but the model is slow and costly. The row must appear instantly, even when the model is having a bad day.

Think of a "you may also like" row.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
20 million people a month
Audience in plain numbers
20,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 15,000 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 93%; Analytics event: 7%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 350 ms
Successful requests
99.5%
Data safety
Best effort: small losses are tolerated.
Monthly budget
≈ $19,000
Data at rest
≈ 3 TB
Where users are
North America: 60%; Europe: 40%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Analytics event: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • A ranking call takes about 50 ms of model time (approx.).
  • Click events help tomorrow's lists but need not be real-time.

Questions that shape the design

Does the row need to be exactly right for this second?

No. A list computed a few hours ago is fine for most people.

What if the model is slow or down?

Show a simple popular-items row. A generic row is far better than a blank space.

Is it a problem if two people see the same row?

No. Many people share a similar taste group, so shared answers are fine.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 12:00 · Slow dependency

    An outside service slows down. Your servers fill with requests waiting on it.

    Added response time: ≈ 3,000 ms. Duration: ≈ 1,800 seconds.

  2. 20:00 · Cache stampede

    The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

    Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

  3. 20:30 · Replication lag

    Copies fall behind. Users read old data, even their own fresh changes.

    Copy lag: ≈ 30 seconds. Duration: ≈ 1,200 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Ranking is expensive. Which rows can be reused between visits?
  • Bound ranking latency and use a compatible fallback when model or features fail.
  • A longer cache time cuts model cost but shows older tastes. A new item takes a while to appear.
  • The breaker trades quality for speed: a generic row is shown when the model is slow.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Remembering answers
  • GPUs, tokens and fallbacks

Related problems

  • Hard

    Ad serving

    Each page view asks you to pick the best ad in about a quarter of a second: check who is allowed to see what, score the candidates with a model, run a quick auction and answer. Every impression and click must be counted exactly because money depends on it.

  • Easy

    Semantic search

    A help center lets people type a question in plain words and finds the right articles even when the words differ. Each question is turned into a list of numbers (a vector) and matched to similar articles. Many people ask the same few questions.

  • Hard

    AI chatbot serving

    Millions of people ask your assistant questions. Each reply takes a GPU several seconds, and GPUs are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Keep replies flowing, protect your wallet from abuse, and have a plan for when the GPUs run out.

  • Easy

    URL shortener

    People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.
